title: How does Kafka guarantee message ordering within a partition, and what happens with multiple consumers (one consumer per partition per group)?
shortTitle: How Kafka guarantees ordering within a partition, and multiple consumers
keyPoints: Ordering is guaranteed per partition because records receive sequential offsets and the partition is immutable and append-only.
Within a consumer group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so no two consumers ever read the same partition concurrently.
The message key determines the partition via hashing, so all records with the same key stay ordered in the same partition.
Producer idempotence (`enable.idempotence=true`) prevents retries from reordering records even with multiple in-flight requests.
More consumers than partitions in a group means the extra consumers sit idle as hot standbys.
Across different consumer groups, each group gets its own independent assignment and reads all partitions without interference.

s1_definition.oneliner: Order is guaranteed per partition because records get sequential offsets and exactly one consumer per group reads each partition.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Partition ordering** – Kafka guarantees that records within a single partition are read in the exact order they were written, because each record receives a sequential offset and the log is immutable.
- **One-consumer-per-partition rule** – within a consumer group, Kafka assigns each partition to exactly one consumer, ensuring no two consumers in the same group read the same partition concurrently.
- **Message key** – the value Kafka hashes to choose the target partition, so all records with the same key land in the same partition and stay ordered relative to each other.
- **Producer idempotence** – the `enable.idempotence=true` setting that makes the broker detect and discard duplicate sends from retries, preserving order even with multiple in-flight requests.
- **Cross-partition ordering** – Kafka makes no ordering guarantee across different partitions; global ordering requires a single-partition topic at the cost of parallelism.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine one drawer of the National Bank of India ledger where pages are glued in sequence: page 0, page 1, page 2. Nobody can shuffle them. Only one clerk is ever allowed to read that drawer for a given team, so the clerk reads page 0, then page 1, then page 2, exactly in order. If the bank added a second clerk to the same team, Kafka would not let both read the same drawer; it hands each clerk a different drawer so there is never a race over the same pages.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Ordering Guarantee Flow
========================

  Producer (key = SAV2001)
      │
      │  send(key="SAV2001", DEBIT)
      │  send(key="SAV2001", CHECK)
      │  send(key="SAV2001", CREDIT)
      │
      ▼
  hash("SAV2001") % 6 = 2
      │
      ▼
  Partition 2:
  ┌──────┬──────┬──────┐
  │ off=0│ off=1│ off=2│
  │DEBIT │CHECK │CREDIT│
  └──────┴──────┴──────┘
      │
      ▼
  Consumer C (settlement-group)
  Reads: DEBIT -> CHECK -> CREDIT (strict order)

  Within Group (one consumer per partition):
  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐  ┌────────────┐
  │ Consumer A │  │ Consumer B │  │ Consumer C │
  │  reads P0  │  │  reads P1  │  │  reads P2  │
  │  reads P3  │  │  reads P4  │  │  reads P5  │
  └────────────┘  └────────────┘  └────────────┘
  No two consumers share a partition = ordering preserved

  Across Groups:
  fraud-group:  reads ALL partitions (own offsets)
  audit-group:  reads ALL partitions (own offsets)
  -> Independent, no interference
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Kafka guarantees message ordering within a partition because each partition is a strictly ordered, append-only, immutable log. When a producer sends records to a partition, Kafka appends them in send order and assigns each a sequential offset. A consumer reads the partition sequentially, so it sees records in exactly the order they were written. This ordering is guaranteed only within a single partition, never across partitions.

The partition a record lands in is chosen by hashing its key. By keying events by account id at National Bank of India, all of Rajesh's transactions land in the same partition and are read in the exact order they happened: his debit always comes before his balance check. The one-consumer-per-partition rule preserves this under parallelism: within a consumer group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so no race condition can break the ordering.

Producer idempotence prevents retries from reordering records. Across different consumer groups, each group gets its own independent assignment and reads all partitions without interfering with other groups. The trade-off is that global ordering requires a single partition, which caps throughput to one consumer.

Remember one sentence: Kafka guarantees ordering within a partition through sequential offsets and the one-consumer-per-partition rule, and the message key is your lever for controlling which records stay ordered together.
